checks.claim: Key: Tycho's own errors (about 1-2 arcminutes) were far smaller than the 8-arcminute gap, so Kepler blamed the model
checks.note: Wikipedia: the vicarious hypothesis matched the oppositions 'to within Tycho's two-arcminute accuracy'; the bisected-eccentricity version's 8' error exceeded Tycho's observational error. Krisciunas (arXiv 1610.05750): Tycho's data 'accurate to +/-2' or better'.

checks.claim: Tycho's accuracy of about one or two arcminutes
checks.note: Grokipedia: instruments gave 'positional accuracies of 0.5 to 2 arcminutes'; Wikipedia: aim 'approaching one arcminute', catalogue median error about 1.5'.

checks.claim: Tycho the last great astronomer to work without a telescope
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the last major astronomer to work without the aid of a telescope'; OpenStax: 'the last and greatest of the pre-telescopic observers in Europe'.

checks.claim: Eight arcminutes is about a quarter of the full Moon's width
checks.note: The Moon is about 30-32 arcminutes across; 8/31 is about a quarter.

checks.claim: Kepler's best circle-based model fit most sightings but missed some by 8 arcminutes, and he threw it out
checks.note: Standard simplification: the vicarious hypothesis (circle with equant) fit the oppositions within 2'; with bisected eccentricity the error rose to 8'. Kepler: 'This hypothesis, so closely in agreement with the observations, is nevertheless false.'

checks.claim: Quotation: 'these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy'
checks.note: Verbatim the English translation Wikipedia gives from Astronomia Nova (ch. 19); other translations word it differently (Britannica, Case Western) but the passage is Kepler's.

checks.claim: Wrong: Ptolemy's old circles had missed by less than that (context: Ptolemaic tables erred by more than 30 arcminutes)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'medieval tables yielded positional errors exceeding 30 arcminutes'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Copernicus's circles had fit those sightings exactly (context: Copernicus used circles, died 1543, long before Tycho's sightings)
checks.note: Grokipedia: died 24 May 1543; kept uniform circular motion and epicycles. Tycho's Mars record runs 1582-1600. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Galileo's telescope had shown the same gap (context: Galileo first turned a telescope on the sky late in 1609, the year Astronomia Nova came out)
checks.note: Grokipedia: first telescope June/July 1609, systematic lunar observation 'in late 1609' (sketches 30 November 1609); Righini argues for early autumn 1609, still the second half of the year. Astronomia Nova 'in print by August 1609'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: an ellipse with the Sun off its centre (at one focus)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the orbit of every planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one of the two foci'; OpenStax the same. A focus lies off the centre.

checks.claim: Set out in Astronomia Nova, 1609
checks.note: Manuscript done 1607, 'in print by August 1609'; Grokipedia: appeared August 1609.

checks.claim: Wrong: an ellipse with the Sun at its centre
checks.note: The Sun is at a focus, not the centre. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: a circle with the Sun off its centre
checks.note: Kepler tried and rejected off-centre circles (the vicarious hypothesis, bisected eccentricity). Truly wrong as his finding.

checks.claim: Wrong: an egg shape with the Sun near its broad end
checks.note: Kepler tried an oval 'slightly wider at the perihelion than at aphelion' and rejected it. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the off-centre circle and the egg each missed by about 8 arcminutes, in opposite directions
checks.note: Wikipedia: the oval showed 'an error of 8 minutes of arc in predicted longitudes'; 'where the bisected eccentricity predicted the planet ahead of its true position, the oval would predict it behind.'

checks.claim: Context: planets' ellipses nearly round; Mars's path drawn to scale looks almost like a circle
checks.note: OpenStax: Mars's orbit drawn to scale is 'practically indistinguishable from a circle'; NASA eccentricity 0.094.

checks.claim: Stem: the shape fit every planet
checks.note: The first law applies to every planet.

checks.claim: Northern winter (December solstice to March equinox) about 89 days; summer (June solstice to September equinox) about 94
checks.note: Wikipedia: 93.65 days June solstice to September equinox; 88.99 days December solstice to March equinox. Grokipedia: 'shorter Northern winter of about 89 days' against 'longer Northern summer of roughly 94 days'. Seasons named correctly.

checks.claim: Earth nearest the Sun in early January, about 147 million km; farthest about 152 million km
checks.note: NASA perihelion 147.1, aphelion 152.1 million km; Grokipedia perihelion around 3 January, aphelion around 4 July.

checks.claim: Key: Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun (Kepler's second law)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the northern winter is shorter because 'the planet moves faster in its elliptical orbit during this period'; Kepler's second law: faster when closer.

checks.claim: Wrong: the Sun's stronger pull in January holds Earth back
checks.note: The planet 'speeds up as it comes closer to the Sun'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Earth's tilt shortens the season tipped away from the Sun
checks.note: The southern winter (June solstice to September equinox, 93.65 days) is the longest season, so the tilt does not shorten winter. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: Earth spins faster on its axis in the winter months
checks.note: Season lengths come from orbital speed, not spin. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: in the south winter is the longest season; the Sun's pull speeds Earth up as it swings in
checks.note: Follows from the 93.65-day June-September interval and the second law.

checks.claim: Saturn about ten times Earth's distance from the Sun
checks.note: 1,432.0 against 149.6 million km = 9.6 times; 'about ten' is a fair rounding.

checks.claim: Saturn's year about 29 Earth years
checks.note: NASA 10,747 days = 29.4 years (often quoted 29.5). 'About 29' is fine.

checks.claim: Key: it moves along its path more slowly than Earth
checks.note: Saturn 9.7 km/s against Earth 29.8 km/s, about a third; ten times the path at the same speed would take only 10 years.

checks.claim: Wrong: its path is stretched into a much longer oval
checks.note: Eccentricity 0.052, nearly round. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: its path climbs far above and below Earth's
checks.note: Inclination 2.5 degrees. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: it winds along its path in small loops
checks.note: Epicycles were Ptolemy's and Copernicus's device; Kepler's ellipses removed them. Truly wrong for the real path round the Sun.

checks.claim: Context: Saturn 9.7 km/s, a third of Earth's 29.8; tilted 2.5 degrees; nearly as round as Earth's
checks.note: Matches NASA.

checks.claim: Context: ten times as far, the pull is a hundredth; a weaker pull holds a planet on its path only at a slower speed
checks.note: Inverse square (10 x 10 = 100); orbital speed 'decreases with increasing orbital radius, as the gravitational pull weakens'.

checks.claim: Context: Ptolemy and Copernicus used epicycles; Kepler's ellipses did away with them
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Copernicus retained epicycles but reduced their overall number'.

checks.claim: Moon about 60 times as far from Earth's centre as an apple at the surface
checks.note: OpenStax: 'The Moon is 60 Earth radii away from the center of Earth.'

checks.claim: The Moon curves toward Earth each second by about 1/3,600 of the apple's first-second drop; Moon about 1.4 mm a second, apple 4.9 m
checks.note: Ohio State: apple 4.9 m in the first second; Moon 0.00136 m (about 1.4 mm); 4.9/3600 = 0.00136. Check by hand: a = 4 pi^2 r / T^2 with r = 384,400 km, T = 27.32 d gives 0.00272 m/s^2, half of which is 1.36 mm.

checks.claim: Key: the pull weakens with the square of the distance
checks.note: Grokipedia: the Moon's acceleration 'equals g/3600', 60^2 = 3600, consistent with an inverse-square law.

checks.claim: Wrong: in step with the distance; with the cube; with the square root
checks.note: These give 1/60, 1/216,000 and 1/7.7, not 1/3,600. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Newton compared the Moon with a falling apple (myth check)
checks.note: Not the apple-on-the-head legend: Conduitt's account from Newton links them directly ('the same power of gravity (wch made an apple fall from the tree to the ground)... Why not as high as the Moon'), and the Principia's Moon test compares the Moon with bodies falling at Earth's surface. Some historians doubt the apple episode itself, so a stricter wording would be 'with a falling body, such as an apple', but the stem as written is defensible.

checks.claim: Context: a pull weakening in step with distance would leave a sixtieth, sixty times too much; twice as far, a quarter as strong
checks.note: Arithmetic correct; OpenStax: twice as far, a quarter of the force.

checks.claim: Jupiter more than 300 times Earth's mass
checks.note: 1,898 against 5.97 x 10^24 kg = 318 times.

checks.claim: In the Principia Newton worked out Jupiter's mass as a share of the Sun's
checks.note: SEP: 'Newton gives theory-dependent answers for Jupiter, Saturn, and the Earth in the corollaries to Proposition 8' (Book 3).

checks.claim: Key: from how fast its moons circle it, at their distances
checks.note: OpenStax: 'the mass of Jupiter by noting the motions of its moons'; Grokipedia (Principia): the four moons' periods 'yield Jupiter's mass as about 1/1,069 of the Sun's'.

checks.claim: Context: about a thousandth of the Sun's mass, close to today's figure; the four moons Galileo found in 1610
checks.note: Newton about 1/1,067-1/1,069 (Maclaurin's account gives 1/1067); today 1,898 x 10^24 / 1.989 x 10^30 = about 1/1,048. Galileo found the moons 7 January 1610 (Grokipedia Galileo).

checks.claim: Wrong: how fast it circles the Sun, at its distance (context: Jupiter trojans share its path and take the same 12 years)
checks.note: Grokipedia: trojans 'share Jupiter's orbit around the Sun', 'orbital periods of about 12 years, identical to Jupiter's'; largest about 225 km. Strictly the period depends on the Sun's mass plus the planet's, so a planet's own year says almost nothing (0.05 percent for Jupiter) of its mass; 'says nothing' is a fair 9th-grade simplification and the choice is truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: how wide it looks; how bright it shines
checks.note: Size and brightness do not give mass. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: The comet took over a year longer between 1531 and 1607 than between 1607 and 1682
checks.note: Wikipedia: the period was 'over a year longer between 1531 and 1607'.

checks.claim: Alexis Clairaut and two fellow mathematicians in Paris (Lalande and Lepaute) computed it before the return
checks.note: Wikipedia names Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute; St Andrews: Clairaut announced to the Paris Academy on 14 November 1758, before the comet was first seen (25 December 1758).

checks.claim: Delay of about 618 days from Jupiter and Saturn
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the attraction of Jupiter and Saturn having caused a retardation of 618 days'; 19th-century accounts (e.g. 'The Story of the Comets') give the computed split: 518 days from Jupiter, 100 from Saturn.

checks.claim: Perihelion 13 March 1759, about a month from their date
checks.note: St Andrews: predicted 15 April 1759, actual perihelion 13 March (Wikipedia gives the prediction as 13 April with a one-month error). Either way, about a month; the stem wisely leaves the predicted date out.

checks.claim: Key: the pull of Jupiter and Saturn as it passed them
checks.note: Grokipedia: the calculation accounted for perturbations from Jupiter and Saturn.

checks.claim: Wrong: drag of thin gas between the planets; push of sunlight on the tail; loss of ice boiled off
checks.note: None was Clairaut's reckoning; Wikipedia: the gas jets cause 'delays in its perihelion passage of four days on average'. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Halley blamed the uneven laps on Jupiter and Saturn; one of the first great tests of Newton's law
checks.note: Wikipedia: Halley found that Jupiter and Saturn could account for the delays; 'one of the earliest successful tests of Newtonian physics'.

checks.claim: Uranus ran ahead of its predicted place, then fell behind
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Uranus appeared to move too quickly before then and too slowly afterward' (about 1821-1822).

checks.claim: Le Verrier in Paris; Galle in Berlin on 23 September 1846 found the planet where Le Verrier said
checks.note: Galle got the letter on the morning of 23 September and found Neptune that night, 'just after midnight', 'less than 1 degree from the position Le Verrier had predicted'. The night of 23-24 September is the standard 23 September date.

checks.claim: Key: an unseen planet farther out was pulling on it
checks.note: Neptune lies beyond Uranus.

checks.claim: Wrong: a planet nearer the Sun; a moon of its own; a passing comet
checks.note: Grokipedia lists unseen rings or satellites among the hypotheses, but Le Verrier's answer was the exterior planet. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Adams worked it out separately in England; Galle and his assistant d'Arrest
checks.note: Grokipedia: Adams 'independently' at Cambridge; d'Arrest 'a young assistant and recent graduate' (Wikipedia: 'a student who was working at the observatory'). 'Assistant' is fine.

checks.claim: Context: some astronomers wondered whether Newton's law failed so far from the Sun; the law held at the edge of the known solar system
checks.note: Wikipedia: one hypothesis was that the Sun's gravity at such distance 'might differ from Newton's description'; the law 'prevailed even at the limits of the Solar System'.

checks.claim: Le Verrier in 1859 found Mercury's perihelion advancing faster than Newton's law and the other planets allow
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 38 arcseconds per century unexplained (later about 43).

checks.claim: He blamed unseen matter closer to the Sun
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'another Mercury-sized planet' or 'an unknown asteroid belt near the Sun'.

checks.claim: Key: Einstein's new theory of gravity (general relativity, 1915), the missing 43 arcseconds a century
checks.note: Wikipedia: general relativity gave '43 arc-seconds per century, exactly the observed amount', as spacetime curvature by the Sun's mass.

checks.claim: Wrong: Asaph Hall's tiny change to the square (1894, exponent 2.00000016), a patch later given up
checks.note: Hall 1894, 'A Suggestion in the Theory of Mercury': exponent about 2.00000016 fits Newcomb's 43''; thatsmaths: 'an ad hoc solution'; arXiv 2402.04643: the same exponent spoiled other results, and it was dropped (Newcomb used it briefly in 1895). Truly wrong as the final answer.

checks.claim: Wrong: a belt of small rocks inside its path; drag from thin gas around the Sun
checks.note: No such matter was found; searches failed. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Newton's law still an excellent guide; relativity needed only for very strong gravity or extreme accuracy
checks.note: Wikipedia: Newton's law 'an excellent approximation' in most applications.

checks.claim: Rod nearly 2 metres long, small lead ball at each end, a lead ball of about 158 kg beside each
checks.note: Wikipedia: six-foot (1.8 m) wooden rod; 1.61-lb (0.73 kg) small spheres; 348-lb (158 kg) large balls.

checks.claim: Earth's own pull on the small balls compared with the big balls' pull
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'the gravitational force of the Earth on the small ball could be measured directly by weighing it'.

checks.claim: 1798: Earth about 5.5 times as dense as water; 5.45 after the slip was corrected; today 5.51
checks.note: Printed 5.48 (5.480); Baily (1821) found the arithmetic slip; correct 5.448; accepted 5.514 g/cm^3. 'About 5.5' is right; the brief's 'about 5.4' would round the corrected figure, but the draft's 5.5 and 5.45 are both accurate.

checks.claim: Key: its inside is far denser than its surface rock (crust about 2.7 to 3)
checks.note: Wikipedia: '80% higher than the density of the Earth's outer crust, suggesting the existence of a dense iron core'; Grokipedia Earth's crust: continental about 2.7, oceanic about 3.0 g/cm^3.

checks.claim: Wrong: as dense as; less dense than; hollow with shells
checks.note: All contradict a mean density about twice the crust's. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Halley suggested in 1692 a hollow Earth with nested shells; no hollow Earth could weigh so much
checks.note: Grokipedia: 1692, outer shell about 500 miles thick, two inner shells and a core; a largely hollow Earth would have about crustal density, so the measured figure rules it out.

checks.claim: Context: with Earth's size the density gives its mass, hence 'weighing the Earth'
checks.note: Correct; Cavendish reported density, not G.

unit_notes: All ten questions pass. Two optional polish points, neither an error: (1) 79ae5124e3 says Newton 'compared the Moon with a falling apple'; this is documented in Conduitt's account from Newton and is not the apple-on-the-head legend, but 'with a falling body, such as an apple' would be bullet-proof. (2) cc74511fe2's context says a planet's own year 'says nothing of its mass'; strictly the period depends on the Sun's mass plus the planet's (0.05 percent for Jupiter), so 'almost nothing' is more exact. Non-player-facing: 12180c2c5f's grade_note calls Cavendish's density 'the first such clue', but the Schiehallion experiment (1774; Hutton 1778) had already given Earth about 4.5 to 5 times water's density (Grokipedia Schiehallion_experiment); the context's 'early evidence' wording is fine. Q4's 'about 29' years (NASA 29.4) and the brief's 29.5 are both fair.
